JEE-MATH-U03-001 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Algebra of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P be a matrix of order 3×2. If Q is a matrix such that both PTQ and QPT are defined, then the order of Q is
  1. (A)3×2
  2. (B)2×3
  3. (C)2×2
  4. (D)3×3
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 3×2

PT has order 2×3. For PTQ to be defined, Q must have 3 rows; for QPT to be defined, Q must have 2 columns. Hence Q is of order 3×2.

Targets: Matching orders for products using P in place of its transpose.
Difficulty: One idea (conformability) applied to two products.
Family: U03-A-order-defined · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-002 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Algebra of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P=[pij​] be the 3×3 matrix with pij​=ij for 1≤i,j≤3. Then the trace of P equals
  1. (A)8
  2. (B)14
  3. (C)32
  4. (D)56
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 32

The trace is p11​+p22​+p33​=11+22+33=1+4+27=32.

Targets: Confusing the main diagonal with the anti-diagonal or with the whole matrix.
Difficulty: Construct the diagonal from a formula and add.

JEE-MATH-U03-004 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Easy · Class XII
If the matrix P=​173​x+2y04​32x−y2​​ is symmetric, where x,y∈R, then x+y equals
  1. (A)−5
  2. (B)5
  3. (C)519​
  4. (D)1
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 5

Symmetry needs p12​=p21​ and p23​=p32​: x+2y=7 and 2x−y=4. From the second, y=2x−4, so x+4x−8=7, giving x=3, y=2 and x+y=5. (Also p13​=p31​=3 holds.)

Targets: Pairing an entry with the wrong mirror entry across the diagonal.
Difficulty: Two linear conditions from the definition of symmetry.
Family: U03-A-symmetric-param · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-005 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Easy · Class XII
If P=​023​αβ4​−3γ0​​ is a skew-symmetric matrix, then α+β+γ equals
  1. (A)−6
  2. (B)−5
  3. (C)6
  4. (D)2
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) −6

For a skew-symmetric matrix pji​=−pij​, so every diagonal entry is 0: β=0. Also α=−p21​=−2 and γ=p23​=−p32​=−4; the pair p13​=−3, p31​=3 is consistent. Hence α+β+γ=−2+0−4=−6.

Targets: Forgetting that diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix are zero, or the sign change.
Difficulty: Direct use of the definition entry by entry.
Family: U03-A-skew-param · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-006 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Algebra of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P and Q be 3×3 matrices with tr(P)=3 and tr(Q)=−2, where tr denotes the trace. Then tr(2PT−3Q) equals
  1. (A)12
  2. (B)0
  3. (C)5
  4. (D)−12
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 12

Trace is linear and tr(PT)=tr(P). So tr(2PT−3Q)=2(3)−3(−2)=6+6=12.

Targets: Thinking transposition changes the trace.
Difficulty: Two trace properties applied once.
Family: U03-A-trace-linear · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-007 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P be a non-zero square matrix with P2=P, and let I be the identity matrix of the same order. If (I+P)3=I+kP, then k equals
  1. (A)6
  2. (B)3
  3. (C)8
  4. (D)7
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 7

Since P and I commute, (I+P)3=I+3P+3P2+P3. With P2=P we get P3=P, so (I+P)3=I+(3+3+1)P=I+7P; thus k=7.

Targets: Mishandling Pn=P in a binomial expansion.
Difficulty: One binomial expansion with one substitution.
Family: U03-A-idempotent-binomial · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-008 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P=[a−6​4b​], where a,b∈R. If P2=I, where I is the 2×2 identity matrix, then ab equals
  1. (A)−24
  2. (B)−25
  3. (C)−23
  4. (D)25
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) −25

P2=[a2−24−6(a+b)​4(a+b)b2−24​]. Equating with I, the off-diagonal entries give a+b=0, so b=−a, and the diagonal gives a2−24=1, so a2=25. Hence ab=−a2=−25 (for both a=5,b=−5 and a=−5,b=5).

Targets: Ignoring the off-diagonal entries of P2, or confusing the involutory condition with P2=O or P2=−I.
Difficulty: One matrix square; the off-diagonal entries force b=−a before the diagonal equation.
Family: U03-A-involutory-trace-zero · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-009 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Easy · Class XII
Let P=[64​−9−6​], and let I and O be the 2×2 identity and null matrices. Then P2026 equals
  1. (A)I
  2. (B)−I

Answer: (D) O

P2=[36−3624−24​−54+54−36+36​]=O. Hence P2026=(P2)1013=O.

JEE-MATH-U03-010 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Powers of matrices · Easy · Class XII
If D=diag(2,−1,3), then the trace of D4 equals
  1. (A)16
  2. (B)98
  3. (C)96
  4. (D)256
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 98

Powers of a diagonal matrix are taken entrywise on the diagonal: D4=diag(16,1,81), so its trace is 16+1+81=98.

Difficulty: One property of diagonal matrices.

JEE-MATH-U03-011 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Counting matrices · Easy · Class XII
The number of 3×3 symmetric matrices whose entries are all from the set {0,1} is
  1. (A)256
  2. (B)64
  3. (C)8
  4. (D)512
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 64

A symmetric 3×3 matrix is fixed by its 3 diagonal entries and the 3 entries above the diagonal; the rest are mirror copies. Each of these 6 entries has 2 choices, giving 26=64.

Targets: Not identifying the independent entries of a symmetric matrix.
Difficulty: Identify 6 free entries and count.

JEE-MATH-U03-013 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Transpose and symmetric matrices · Easy · Class XII
Statement I: For every square matrix P, the matrix P+PT is symmetric. Statement II: For every square matrix P, the matrix PPT is skew-symmetric. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  2. (B)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  3. (C)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

(P+PT)T=PT+P, so Statement I is true. (PPT)T=(PT)TPT=PPT, so PPT is symmetric, not skew-symmetric (for example, if P=I then PPT=I=−I); Statement II is false.

Targets: Confusing PPT (symmetric) with P−PT (skew-symmetric).
Difficulty: Two one-line transpose checks.
Family: U03-A-stmt-sym-constructions · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-017 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Counting matrices · Easy · Class XII
The number of 3×3 skew-symmetric matrices whose entries are all from the set {−1,0,1} is
  1. (A)8
  2. (B)729
  3. (C)27
  4. (D)19683
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 27

For a skew-symmetric matrix the diagonal entries are 0 and each entry below the diagonal is the negative of its mirror entry. The 3 entries above the diagonal are free, each with 3 choices (their negatives also lie in the set), giving 33=27.

Targets: Forgetting that diagonal entries of a skew-symmetric matrix must be zero.
Difficulty: Identify the free entries and count.

JEE-MATH-U03-018 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Algebra of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Let P=[13​24​] and Q=[a6​4b​], where a,b∈R. If PQ=QP, then b−a equals
  1. (A)6
  2. (B)18
  3. (C)−6
  4. (D)12
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 6

PQ=[a+123a+24​4+2b12+4b​] and QP=[a+126+3b​2a+1612+4b​]. The (1,2) entries give 2b−2a=12 and the (2,1) entries give 3b−3a=18; both say b−a=6. So a,b are not unique, but b−a=6.

JEE-MATH-U03-019 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Powers of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Let P=[20​12​]. For a positive integer n, write Pn=[α0​βα​]. If β=6α, then n equals
  1. (A)3
  2. (B)12
  3. (C)6
  4. (D)13
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 12

Write P=2I+N with N=[00​10​]. Since N2=O and 2I commutes with N, the binomial expansion gives Pn=2nI+n2n−1N=[2n0​n2n−12n​]. So α=2n, β=n2n−1 and αβ​=2n​=6, giving n=12.

JEE-MATH-U03-020 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Powers of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Let P=​111​011​001​​. The entry in the third row and first column of P10 is
  1. (A)10
  2. (B)55

  4. (D)45
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 55

Write P=I+N with N=​011​001​000​​. Then N2 has a single non-zero entry 1 in position (3,1) and N3=O. Since I and N commute, P10=I+10N+(210​)N2, whose (3,1) entry is 10+45=55.

JEE-MATH-U03-021 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Powers of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Let P=[cos12π​sin12π​​−sin12π​cos12π​​]. The least positive integer n for which Pn=I is
  1. (A)24
  2. (B)48
  3. (C)6
  4. (D)12
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 24

P is the rotation matrix R(θ) with θ=12π​, and R(α)R(β)=R(α+β), so Pn=R(12nπ​). This is I exactly when 12nπ​ is a multiple of 2π, so the least n is 24.

JEE-MATH-U03-022 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Powers of matrices · Medium · Class XII

  1. (A)15
  2. (B)81

P2=3P, since each entry of P2 is 1+1+1. Then P3=3P2=9P and in general Pn=3n−1P, so P5=81P and k=81.

P2=[9−1−3−2​3+2−1+4​]=[8−5​53​]. Comparing with αP+βI=[3α+β−α​α2α+β​] gives α=5 and 15+β=8, so β=−7. Hence α+β=−2.

JEE-MATH-U03-024 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Transpose and symmetric matrices · Medium · Class XII
The matrix P=​237​50−2​−141​​ is written as S+K, where S is symmetric and K is skew-symmetric. The sum of the squares of all nine entries of K is
  1. (A)104

K=21​(P−PT). Its entries above the diagonal are k12​=25−3​=1, k13​=2−1−7​=−4, k23​=24+2​=3; the diagonal is zero and the entries below are the negatives. The sum of squares is 2(1+16+9)=52.

JEE-MATH-U03-025 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Transpose and symmetric matrices · Medium · Class XII
Statement I: If P and Q are symmetric matrices of the same order with PQ=QP, then PQ is symmetric. Statement II: If P is a skew-symmetric matrix, then P3 is skew-symmetric. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  2. (B)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

Statement I: (PQ)T=QTPT=QP=PQ, so PQ is symmetric; true. Statement II: (P3)T=(PT)3=(−P)3=−P3, so P3 is skew-symmetric; true.

Targets: Assuming all powers of a skew-symmetric matrix are symmetric (only even powers are).
Difficulty: Two short transpose arguments, one needing the commuting hypothesis.
Family: U03-A-stmt-sym-products · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-026 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Statement I: If P and Q are idempotent matrices of the same order (that is, P2=P and Q2=Q), then PQ is idempotent. Statement II: If P is idempotent, then I−P is idempotent, where I is the identity matrix of the same order. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  2. (B)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Statement I is false: P=[10​00​] and Q=[00​11​] are idempotent, but PQ=[00​10​] has (PQ)2=O=PQ. Statement II is true: (I−P)2=I−2P+P2=I−2P+P=I−P.

Targets: Using (PQ)2=P2Q2, valid only when P and Q commute.
Difficulty: Needs a counterexample for one statement and a short expansion for the other.
Family: U03-A-stmt-idempotent · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-027 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Algebra of matrices · Medium · Class XII
Statement I: For all square matrices P and Q of the same order, (P+Q)2=P2+2PQ+Q2. Statement II: If P and Q are square matrices of the same order with PQ=O, then P=O or Q=O. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  2. (B)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  3. (C)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

(P+Q)2=P2+PQ+QP+Q2, which equals P2+2PQ+Q2 only when PQ=QP; for P=[00​10​], Q=[01​00​] it fails, so Statement I is false. For P=[10​00​], Q=[00​01​] we have PQ=O with both non-zero, so Statement II is false.

Targets: Applying real-number algebra rules to matrices.
Difficulty: Requires constructing two counterexamples.
Family: U03-A-stmt-noncommutative · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-028 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Types of matrices · Medium · Class XII
If P=31​​12a​212​2−2b​​ satisfies PPT=I, where a,b∈R, then a+b equals
  1. (A)3
  2. (B)−3
  3. (C)−31​
  4. (D)1
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) −3

PPT=I means the rows of 3P are mutually orthogonal and each has length 3. Orthogonality of row 3 to rows 1 and 2 gives a+4+2b=0 and 2a+2−2b=0, i.e. a=b−1 and then 3b+3=0, so b=−1, a=−2. The length check 4+4+1=9 holds. Hence a+b=−3.

Targets: Using only part of the orthogonality conditions.

Answer and solution

Answer: (A) 12

Let P=[ac​bd​]. Comparing entries of P2=P gives b(a+d−1)=0, c(a+d−1)=0, a2+bc=a and d2+bc=d. If a+d=1, then b=c=0 and a2=a, d2=d, so a,d∈{0,1} with a=d (since a+d=1): only O and I. If a+d=1, then bc=a−a2=a(1−a)=ad; with entries in {0,1,2}, a+d=1 forces (a,d)=(1,0) or (0,1), so ad=0 and bc=0: 5 pairs (b,c) each, giving 10. Total 10+2=12.

R(α)R(β)=R(α+β), so R(θ)3=R(3θ), and R(θ)T=R(−θ). Thus R(3θ)=R(−θ), i.e. cos3θ=cosθ and sin3θ=−sinθ, which means 4θ=2kπ. In [0,2π): θ=0,2π​,π,23π​, so there are 4 values.

Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 2320−1​

Every power of P has the form [αn​βn​​βn​αn​​]. Multiplying by P gives αn+1​=2αn​+βn​ and βn+1​=αn​+2βn​, so αn+1​+βn+1​=3(αn​+βn​) and αn+1​−βn+1​=αn​−βn​. With α1​=2,β1​=1 this gives αn​+βn​=3n and αn​−βn​=1. Hence β20​=2320−1​.

Let P be any square matrix of order 3. Statement I: ∣PT∣=∣P∣. Statement II: ∣−P∣=∣P∣. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.

  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Transposing does not change a determinant, so Statement I is true. For order 3, ∣−P∣=(−1)3∣P∣=−∣P∣, which differs from ∣P∣ whenever ∣P∣=0, so Statement II is false.

Statement I: For every square matrix P of order 3, ∣P+PT∣=2∣P∣. Statement II: If a square matrix of order 3 has determinant zero, then it has a zero row or two proportional rows. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  2. (B)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

Statement I: for P=​000​100​001​​, ∣P∣=0 but ∣P+PT∣=​010​100​002​​=−2, so it is false. Statement II: ​101​011​112​​ has R3​=R1​+R2​, so its determinant is 0, yet no row is zero and no two rows are proportional. Both are false.

The sides 3,4,5 form a right triangle of area 21​⋅3⋅4=6. The determinant equals ±2×area=±12, so its square is 144, independent of position and orientation.

Statement I: For every square matrix P of order 3, adj(PT)=(adjP)T. Statement II: For all invertible matrices P and Q of order 3, adj(PQ)=(adjP)(adjQ). In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  2. (B)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

The cofactor of the (i,j) entry of PT equals the cofactor of the (j,i) entry of P, so adj(PT)=(adjP)T; Statement I is true. For invertible P,Q, adj(PQ)=∣PQ∣(PQ)−1=∣Q∣Q−1⋅∣P∣P−1=(adjQ)(adjP), with the order reversed, and in general this differs from (adjP)(adjQ); Statement II is false.

Targets: Forgetting the reversal of order for the adjoint of a product.
Difficulty: Two adjoint properties, one needing the reversal law.
Family: U03-C-stmt-adj-props · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

JEE-MATH-U03-136 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Adjoint and inverse · Medium · Class XII
Statement I: If P is an invertible symmetric matrix, then P−1 is symmetric. Statement II: If P is an invertible upper triangular matrix of order 3, then P−1 is upper triangular. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  2. (B)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  3. (C)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
  4. (D)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) Both Statement I and Statement II are true

If PT=P, then (P−1)T=(PT)−1=P−1, so Statement I is true. For upper triangular P with non-zero diagonal, each cofactor Cij​ with i<j is the determinant of a triangular block with a zero on its diagonal, so it vanishes; after transposing, the adjoint and hence P−1=∣P∣adjP​ have zeros below the diagonal. Statement II is true.

Targets: Thinking inversion changes symmetric or triangular structure.
Difficulty: Two structural facts about inverses.

JEE-MATH-U03-137 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Adjoint and inverse · Medium · Class XII
Statement I: If P is a non-zero skew-symmetric matrix of order 2, then P−1 is symmetric. Statement II: If P is a skew-symmetric matrix of order 3, then adjP is skew-symmetric. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.
  1. (A)Statement I is true but Statement II is false
  2. (B)Both Statement I and Statement II are true
  3. (C)Statement I is false but Statement II is true
  4. (D)Both Statement I and Statement II are false
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) Both Statement I and Statement II are false

For P=[0−p​p0​] with p=0, (P−1)T=(PT)−1=−P−1, so P−1=[0p1​​−p1​0​] is skew-symmetric, not symmetric (it is non-zero). Statement I is false. For order 3, adj(PT)=(adjP)T and adj(−P)=(−1)2adjP, so (adjP)T=adj(−P)=adjP: the adjoint is symmetric. For example ​0−1−2​10−3​230​​ has the non-zero symmetric adjoint ​9−63​−64−2​3−21​​. Statement II is false.

Statement I: Every non-zero square matrix P with P2=P is invertible. Statement II: If P is a non-singular matrix and PQ=PR for matrices Q,R of the same order, then Q=R. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.

Answer: (B) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

P=[10​00​] is non-zero and satisfies P2=P, but ∣P∣=0; Statement I is false (cancelling P needs P−1, which is what is in question). If P is non-singular, pre-multiplying PQ=PR by P−1 gives Q=R; Statement II is true.

Every square matrix P of order 2 satisfies P2−(trP)P+∣P∣I=O. Let P be a real matrix of order 2 such that P−1=P, P=I and P=−I. Then ​adjP+3P−1​ equals

Answer: (C) −4

Since P2=I, the given identity becomes (trP)P=(1+∣P∣)I. If trP=0, P would be a scalar matrix λI with λ2=1, i.e. P=±I, which is excluded. So trP=0 and ∣P∣=−1. Then adjP=∣P∣P−1=−P and P−1=P, so adjP+3P−1=2P and ∣2P∣=22∣P∣=−4.

JEE-MATH-U03-154 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Adjoint and inverse · Difficult · Class XII
Let P be a real, non-singular, non-symmetric matrix of order 3 such that PPT=PTP, and let Q=P−1PT. Then, for every such P, QQT necessarily equals
  1. (A)QT
  2. (B)I
  3. (C)Q

Answer and solution

Answer: (B) I

QT=(PT)T(P−1)T=P(PT)−1. So QQT=P−1PTP(PT)−1=P−1(PPT)(PT)−1, using PTP=PPT. This is (P−1P)(PT(PT)−1)=I. (Note Q=I, since Q=I would force PT=P; so neither Q nor QT=Q−1 can equal I, and QQT has non-negative diagonal entries, so it is never −I.)

JEE-MATH-U03-160 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Adjoint and inverse · Difficult · Class XII
The number of 2×2 matrices with every entry from {0,1,2} that are invertible and whose inverse has all entries integers is
  1. (A)50
  2. (B)14
  3. (C)7
  4. (D)38
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) 14

An integer matrix has an integer inverse exactly when its determinant is ±1 (since ∣P∣∣P−1∣=1 with both integers, and adjP is an integer matrix). With P=[pr​qs​], the product ps takes the values 0,1,2,4 in 5,1,2,1 ways respectively, and the same holds for qr. ps−qr=1 needs (ps,qr)=(1,0) or (2,1): 1⋅5+2⋅1=7 ways. By symmetry ps−qr=−1 also has 7. Total 14.

Targets: Missing the negative determinant or forgetting that the integer condition forces ∣P∣=±1.
Difficulty: Needs the determinant criterion and careful casework counting.

JEE-MATH-U03-161 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Adjoint and inverse · Difficult · Class XII
Let S be a non-zero real skew-symmetric matrix of order 3 (so that I+S is invertible), and let M=(I−S)(I+S)−1. Which of the following is true?

  2. (B)MT=M
  3. (C)∣M∣=−1
  4. (D)M2=I
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) MMT=I

I−S and (I+S)−1 commute, since I−S and I+S commute. MT=((I+S)−1)T(I−S)T=(I−S)−1(I+S), using ST=−S. Then MMT=(I−S)(I+S)−1(I−S)−1(I+S)=I. Also ∣M∣=∣I+S∣∣I−S∣​=1 because I−S=(I+S)T. Finally M2=I would give (I−S)2=(I+S)2, that is S=O, and MT=M is equivalent to M2=I here; both fail for non-zero S.

Targets: Mishandling transpose and inverse of products.
Difficulty: Transpose and inverse of a product with commuting factors, plus exclusion of three claims.

JEE-MATH-U03-171 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Easy · Class XII
Let P be a 3×3 matrix, X=​xyz​​ and O the 3×1 zero matrix. Statement I: The homogeneous system PX=O is always consistent. Statement II: If ∣P∣=0, then the system PX=O has infinitely many solutions. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.

  4. (D)Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Answer: (D) Statement I is true but Statement II is false

Statement I is true because X=O always satisfies PX=O. Statement II is false: if ∣P∣=0, then P−1 exists and X=P−1O=O is the only solution, so the system has only the trivial solution.

JEE-MATH-U03-174 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Easy · Class XII
For a system of three linear equations in three unknowns, let Δ be the determinant of the coefficient matrix and Δ1​,Δ2​,Δ3​ the determinants obtained by replacing its first, second and third columns by the constants. If Δ=0 and at least one of Δ1​,Δ2​,Δ3​ is non-zero, then the system

  2. (B)has only the trivial solution
  3. (C)has no solution
  4. (D)has infinitely many solutions
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) has no solution

If a solution existed, Cramer's relations xΔ=Δ1​, yΔ=Δ2​, zΔ=Δ3​ would hold. With Δ=0 the left sides are all 0, contradicting a non-zero Δi​. Hence the system is inconsistent and has no solution.

Answer and solution

Answer: (D) only when k=−2

Δ=(k−1)2(k+2). For k=1 every equation is x+y+z=1, so there are infinitely many solutions. For k=−2, adding the equations gives (k+2)(x+y+z)=1+k+k2, i.e. 0=3, a contradiction. So the system has no solution only for k=−2.

The system x+y+z=a, x+2y+3z=b, x+3y+5z=c is consistent if and only if
  1. (A)a,b,c are in A.P.
  2. (B)a+b=c
  3. (C)a,b,c are in G.P.
  4. (D)a,b,c are in H.P.
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) a,b,c are in A.P.

The coefficient rows satisfy R1​+R3​=(2,4,6)=2R2​, so Δ=0 and every solution would force a+c=2b. Conversely, if a+c=2b, the third equation follows from the first two, which are independent, so solutions exist. Hence the system is consistent exactly when a,b,c are in A.P.

Let P be a 3×3 matrix, Q a 3×1 matrix and X=​xyz​​. Statement I: If ∣P∣=0 and (adjP)Q=O, then the system PX=Q has infinitely many solutions. Statement II: If ∣P∣=0, then the system PX=Q has the unique solution X=P−1Q. In the light of the above statements, choose the correct answer.

Answer: (B) Statement I is false but Statement II is true

Statement I is false. Take x+y+z=1, x+y+z=2, x+y+z=3: every 2×2 minor of the all-ones matrix P is 0, so adjP=O, ∣P∣=0 and (adjP)Q=O, yet the system is clearly inconsistent. Statement II is true: if ∣P∣=0, then P−1 exists, X=P−1Q satisfies PX=Q, and any solution must equal P−1Q.

JEE-MATH-U03-210 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
For k>0, the system x+ky+z=0, x+y+kz=0, 3x+2y−2z=0 has a non-trivial solution (x,y,z). Then zx+2y​ equals
  1. (A)−6
  2. (B)−14
  3. (C)14
  4. (D)2
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) −6

Δ=1(−2−2k)−k(−2−3k)+1(2−3)=3k2−3=3(k−1)(k+1), so k=1. The equations become x+y+z=0 and 3x+2y−2z=0. Cross-multiplying: x:y:z=(−2−2):(3+2):(2−3)=−4:5:−1, i.e. 4:−5:1. So zx+2y​=14−10​=−6.

Targets: Sign slips in cross-multiplication, or ignoring the condition k>0.

JEE-MATH-U03-211 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
The system x+y+kz=0, kx+2y+z=0, x−y+z=0 has a non-trivial solution in which x, y and z are all positive. Then k equals
  1. (A)4
  2. (B)−4
  3. (C)−2
  4. (D)1
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) −4

Δ=1(2+1)−1(k−1)+k(−k−2)=−k2−3k+4=−(k−1)(k+4), so k=1 or k=−4. For k=1, the solutions are multiples of (−1,0,1), not all positive. For k=−4, the equations x+y−4z=0 and x−y+z=0 give x:y:z=3:5:2, all positive. Hence k=−4.

Targets: Stopping at Δ=0 without testing each root against the extra condition.

JEE-MATH-U03-212 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
The number of integers k in [−5,5] for which the system x+ky+z=1, kx+y−z=0, x+y+kz=1 has at least one solution is
  1. (A)8
  2. (B)2
  3. (C)11
  4. (D)10
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 10

Δ=1(k+1)−k(k2+1)+1(k−1)=−k3+k=−k(k−1)(k+1). For k=0: x+z=1, y−z=0, x+y=1, consistent (infinitely many). For k=1: x+y+z=1 and x+y−z=0, consistent. For k=−1: the first two equations are x−y+z=1 and −x+y−z=0, and adding them gives 0=1, so the system is inconsistent. So 11−1=10 integers work.

Targets: Treating every root of Δ as a failure of solvability.
Difficulty: Cubic determinant and consistency tests at three roots, then counting.

JEE-MATH-U03-213 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
Let p and q be positive integers. The number of ordered pairs (p,q) for which the system x+2y−z=p, 2x−y+3z=q, 4x+3y+z=pq−4 is consistent is
  1. (A)3
  2. (B)8
  3. (C)4
  4. (D)0
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 4

Since 2(1,2,−1)+(2,−1,3)=(4,3,1), the rows satisfy R3​=2R1​+R2​, so Δ=0; as R1​ and R2​ are independent, the system is consistent if and only if pq−4=2p+q. Adding 2 to both sides of pq−2p−q=4 gives (p−1)(q−2)=6. For positive integers p−1≥0 and the product is positive, so p−1 and q−2 form a positive divisor pair of 6: (1,6), (2,3), (3,2), (6,1). Hence (p,q)=(2,8), (3,5), (4,4), (7,3), which is 4 pairs.

Targets: Mishandling the factorisation pq−2p−q=(p−1)(q−2)−2, or ignoring the positivity condition.
Difficulty: Row relation for a singular system, a factorisation trick on the constants, and a constrained divisor count.
Family: U03-D-consistency-integer-pairs · Check: MACHINE_RECOMPUTED; BLIND_RESOLVED; EDITORIAL_AUDITED; ERRATA_RECOMPUTED; ERRATA_AUDITED

The set of all real values of k for which the system x+2y+3z=1, 2x+ky+6z=2, 3x+6y+k2z=4 has no solution is
  1. (A){−3,3}
  2. (B){4}
  3. (C){−3,3,4}
  4. (D){3}
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) {−3,3}

Δ=1(k3−36)−2(2k2−18)+3(12−3k)=k3−4k2−9k+36=(k−4)(k−3)(k+3). At k=4 the second equation is twice the first, and the remaining two equations are independent, so there are infinitely many solutions. At k=±3 the third coefficient row is (3,6,9)=3R1​, but the constant is 4=3, so there is no solution. Hence the set is {−3,3}.

Targets: Equating Δ=0 with no solution.
Difficulty: Cubic determinant and a separate consistency check at each of three roots.

The sum of all distinct real values of k for which the equations kx+y=1, x+ky=1 and x+y=k have a common solution is
  1. (A)0
  2. (B)−1
  3. (C)1
  4. (D)−2
Answer and solution

Answer: (B) −1

A common solution needs ​k11​1k1​11k​​=(k−1)2(k+2)=0. For k=1 all three equations are x+y=1, so they have common solutions. For k=−2: −2x+y=1 and x−2y=1 give x=y=−1, and x+y=−2=k holds. Both values work, and their sum is 1+(−2)=−1.

The system x+y+z=10, x+2y+3z=15, 3x+4y+λz=μ has infinitely many solutions. The number of these solutions (x,y,z) in which x, y, z are all non-negative integers is
  1. (A)6
  2. (B)2
  3. (C)3
  4. (D)4
Answer and solution

Answer: (C) 3

Δ=1(2λ−12)−1(λ−9)+1(4−6)=λ−5, so λ=5, with R3​=2R1​+R2​ and μ=35. The solutions satisfy R2​−R1​: y+2z=5, so y=5−2z and x=10−y−z=5+z. Non-negativity needs 0≤z≤25​, so z=0,1,2, giving (5,5,0), (6,3,1), (7,1,2). That is 3 solutions.

JEE-MATH-U03-218 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
For real d, let (x,y,z) be the solution of x+y+z=1, x+2y+3z=d, x+4y+9z=d2. The set of all d for which x>0 and y>0 is
  1. (A)(1,2)
  2. (B)(−∞,2)∪(3,∞)
  3. (C)(1,3)
  4. (D)(2,3)
Answer and solution

Answer: (A) (1,2)

Δ=(2−1)(3−1)(3−2)=2 (a Vandermonde determinant). Cramer's rule gives x=2(d−2)(d−3)​ and y=−(d−1)(d−3). Then y>0⟺1<d<3, and x>0⟺d<2 or d>3. Both hold exactly for 1<d<2.

Targets: Dropping one of the two sign conditions, or a sign slip in Cramer's rule.
Difficulty: Solving with a parameter, then combining two quadratic inequalities.

JEE-MATH-U03-219 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
Let P=​112​12β​1α4​​, where α,β are real. If X1​=​111​​ and X2​=​2−12​​ are both solutions of PX=Q for some 3×1 matrix Q, then the system PX=​2k7​​ is consistent if and only if k equals
  1. (A)9
  2. (B)29​
  3. (C)−5
  4. (D)5
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 5

From PX1​=PX2​=Q we get P(X2​−X1​)=O with X2​−X1​=(1,−2,1). The second row gives 1−4+α=0, so α=3; the third gives 2−2β+4=0, so β=3. Now the rows (1,1,1), (1,2,3), (2,3,4) satisfy R3​=R1​+R2​ while R1​ and R2​ are independent, so PX=(2,k,7)T is consistent exactly when 7=2+k, that is k=5.

Targets: Confusing the column relation P(X2​−X1​)=O with the row relation that governs consistency.
Difficulty: Uses two solutions to recover unknown entries, then switches from a column relation to a row relation for a new right-hand side.

JEE-MATH-U03-220 · Unit 3: Matrices and Determinants · Systems of linear equations · Difficult · Class XII
The number of integers k with 1≤k≤50 for which the solution of the system x+y+z=6, x+2y+3z=k, x−y+2z=5 has x, y, z all integers is
  1. (A)50
  2. (B)9
  3. (C)40
  4. (D)10
Answer and solution

Answer: (D) 10

Δ=1(4+3)−1(2−3)+1(−1−2)=5. Cramer's rule gives x=547−3k​, y=5k−4​, z=52k−13​. All three are integers exactly when k≡4(mod5) (then 47−3k≡35 and 2k−13≡−5, both multiples of 5). In [1,50] these are k=4,9,…,49: 10 values.

Difficulty: Cramer's rule with a parameter, a divisibility condition and a count.
